For a long time neither of them moved. The lantern hissed. Frost crept back over the ground wherever the dragon's breath did not reach, and Ailis, who had been cold for hours, realised she was no longer cold at all. The great grey head lay beside her like a fallen standing stone, and the warmth coming off it was steady and patient, the warmth of a hearth that did not care who sat beside it.

She should have run. Every story she had ever heard in the toll-house kitchen said so. But her legs had stopped belonging to her somewhere around midnight, and when she finally did move, it was not away. She sat down. She put the lantern on the ground between her knees, and after a while she leaned back against the dragon's foreleg, which was the only warm thing left in the world, and she slept.

She woke to someone saying her name. An old woman was standing at the edge of the clearing with a shepherd's crook in one hand and a lantern of her own in the other, unlit now in the grey morning. She was thin as a fence rail and wrapped in a patched oilskin, and she was staring at the dragon with an expression the girl had never seen on an adult face. It was not fear. It was recognition.

The woman's name was Tamsin. Everyone in Carrow Ford knew that name, the way you know the name of a ghost. Tamsin had kept the lamps along the ford road for thirty winters, until the spring she stood up in the market and told the whole town that the old river wall was rotten and would fail in the next flood. Nobody believed her. The wall failed. Three houses went into the river, and the town, needing someone to blame, decided she must have cursed it. They drove her out into the Reach, and they told their children she had been eaten long ago.

Ailis knew the stories. Tamsin was the witch of the Reach, the one who whistled up floods, the one you did not name after dark. Looking at her now, Ailis saw only a tired old woman with frost in her eyebrows and kindness in her hands.

She had not been eaten. She had been living in a stone hut at the head of the valley, and in all that time, she said, the grey one had never once come close to a human being. Until now.

Tamsin crouched in front of Ailis, slowly, the way you approach a frightened horse. May I see it, she asked, and she touched her own collarbone to show what she meant. Ailis hesitated. Her whole life she had been taught to keep the mark covered. Then she thought of her mother walking away without turning around, and she understood that the person who had taught her to hide it was not coming back to scold her. She unbuttoned the high collar.

Tamsin looked at the whorl for a long moment. It was a small thing, a spiral of rust-red skin no bigger than a coin, with three short lines running out from one side like the ribs of a wing. The old woman's lips moved without sound. I have seen this, she said at last. Not on a person. On a stone. Carved, a very long time ago, by people who knew what it meant.

The dragon lifted her head and looked at them both. Where, Ailis asked. Where is the stone? Tamsin glanced toward the river, still hidden beyond the ridge, swollen with autumn rain. Under the water, she said. At the ford. We cannot reach it until the river drops. And by then, child, somebody in your mother's house will already be telling the town that you are dead.
